THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Indian Ocean Monsoon Trade Before European Sails

Unlike Atlantic navigation across steady trade winds, the Indian Ocean reverses direction twice every year: Northeast winds drive dhows southward from Arabia toward East Africa and western India in winter, while fierce Southwest monsoons sweep cargoes homeward each summer.

Covers maritime archaeology, plant translocations, port custom laws, and shipwreck assemblages from c. 100 BCE to 1500 CE.

Sewn planks, teak hulls, and botanical travelers

Excavations at Berenike in Egypt and Qana in southern Arabia uncover coconut coir cordage, Indian cotton sailcloth fragments, and peppercorns traveling westward alongside African frankincense, Ethiopian ivory, and Mediterranean coinage. [1] [2]

Across centuries, sailors also carried living crops—bananas, taro, Asian rice, sorghum, pearl millet, mung bean—reshaping East African, Comorian, and Malagasy farming landscapes. [6] [2]

Segmented voyages across three monsoon seas

Rather than single vessels sailing door-to-door from Suez to Canton, most exchange operated across linked arenas meeting at Gujarat, Malabar, Srivijaya/Palembang, and Melaka—ports governed by written admiralty codes balancing polyglot guilds. [3] [4] [5]

Coastal cities between interior kingdoms and ocean winds

Harbors like Adulis, Kilwa, Kozhikode, and Quanzhou functioned as specialized ecological hinges rather than isolated islands: highland Aksumite ivory, Great Zimbabwe gold, Cardamom Hill pepper, and Jingdezhen porcelain converged at coastal wharves timed to biannual sailings. [1] [4] [7]
